issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Rajiv's eyes would often dart towards the mirror in his nursing station, a habitual gesture he couldn't shake off. He'd check his surroundings, scanning the ward for any signs of potential threat, just as he had been doing for months now. It was a coping mechanism, one that helped him feel slightly more in control. But deep down, Rajiv knew it was a losing battle – nothing good could happen to him anymore. The mugging that had left him with a broken rib and a shattered sense of security still lingered, refusing to be erased from his memory. The event itself was etched in his mind like a series of photographs – the glint of metal, the sound of footsteps, the feeling of being trapped. When these memories resurfaced, Rajiv would feel the same physical pain he had experienced that night, as if his body was reliving the trauma. He'd become convinced that there was something inherently faulty about him, something that made him a target for such violence. This self-doubt seeped into every aspect of his life, making him question whether he was truly cut out to be a nurse. Rajiv's sleep problems began shortly after the incident. He would lie awake at night, replaying the events in his head, wondering what he could have done differently. His mind occupied with worst-case scenarios, he'd get up and check on his family, making sure they were safe. This constant vigilance left him exhausted but also fueled his hypervigilance during the day. At work, he'd always choose a seat that allowed him to keep an eye on the door, just in case someone suspicious walked in. The memories of that night continued to haunt Rajiv, and with each recollection, his negative self-talk intensified. He became more withdrawn, avoiding social interactions for fear of being hurt again. His family tried to reassure him, but Rajiv was convinced that he had no future ahead of him – the incident had ruined everything. This hopelessness further entrenched his maladaptive strategies, as if checking his surroundings or mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios could somehow undo the past. As time passed, these coping mechanisms began to take a toll on Rajiv's relationships and work performance. His wife complained about his constant distraction, while his colleagues grew concerned about his ability to focus on patients. It was only when he received a written warning from hospital administration that Rajiv realized he needed help – the cycle of fear, self-doubt, and hypervigilance had become too much to bear. Rajiv's greatest fear now is that he'll never be able to break free from this cycle, that he'll remain forever trapped in this state of heightened anxiety. He hopes that therapy will help him untangle the web of negative thoughts and memories, allowing him to rebuild a sense of purpose and security. As he prepares for his first session, Rajiv can't help but wonder – what if nothing good can indeed happen to him anymore?
